name: Spherical code, 58 points in dimension 3
description: Place 58 points on the unit sphere in R^3 so that the smallest angle between two of them is as large as possible (the Tammes problem). The angle between two points is the angle at the centre of the sphere, the arccosine of the inner product of the two unit vectors.
contract: construct() -> array of shape (58, 3): one point per row (the verifier scales every row to unit length; a zero or non-finite row is invalid). Score: smallest angle between two points in degrees, maximized.
notes: The code listed for this size in Cohn's table of spherical codes reaches 27.556415956 degrees (computed by this task's verifier from the table's coordinates, read 2026-11-15). Sloane's table of 1994-96, the source of the first version of this task, lists a code with the same angle.

No data files are needed to run the task. The record comes from the coordinates at https://spherical-codes.org/data/3/58, which only the record validation reads (scripts/new_open_problems/prepare_new_data.py --family sphere).
Spherical code with 58 points in R^3, scored by the smallest pairwise angle; the reference is the code listed for this size in Cohn's table of spherical codes.
The listed code is the best known one, found by computer search and not proven optimal (sizes that are proven have no task).
The table is updated all the time: codes of this family were improved in 2022 to 2026. The record is the state on 2026-11-15 and will fall behind.
A result counts as an improvement only above the record by more than 1e-5 degrees, a margin against numerical slack in the listed coordinates.

Wang, Finding and investigating exact spherical codes: the preprint of the paper cited above, the version that was read.
Musin and Tarasov (2012), The Strong Thirteen Spheres Problem: solves the Tammes problem for n = 13 in R^3 (the main suite task math-tammes-sphere-13-points uses it); not an n of this family.
Musin and Tarasov (2015), The Tammes Problem for N = 14: computer-assisted proof for n = 14 in R^3; the family starts at n = 16.
mt0-svg (2026), The Tammes problem for fifteen points: a preprint, not peer reviewed, on whose strength Cohn's table marks n = 15 in R^3 as optimal; that size has no task for this reason.
Bachoc and Vallentin, Optimality and uniqueness of the (4,10,1/6) spherical code: semidefinite-programming proof for 10 points in R^4; the family starts at n = 11 there.

Leijenhorst (2025), On the computation of three and four-point bounds in discrete geometry and analytic number theory (doctoral thesis, TU Delft): cited by Cohn's table for the optimality of 12 points in R^4, a size the family leaves out for this reason.

Cohn and Kumar (2007), Universally optimal distribution of points on spheres: proves optimality of special codes such as the 600-cell (4, 120) and the 5-dimensional 16-point code, which the family leaves out.

science_relevance.reason: Both papers have the densest packing of n equal circles on a sphere, for whole ranges of n, as their main objective; the task poses the same problem for one n.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Place 58 points on the unit sphere in R^3 so that the smallest angular distance between two points is as large as possible (the Tammes problem, equivalently the densest packing of 58 equal circles on a sphere).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: The Tammes problem asks how to spread points on a sphere as far apart as possible; it arose from the arrangement of pores on pollen grains and models the stereochemistry of atoms around a central atom, the placing of dimples, sensors and viewing directions, and spherical codes. Optimal arrangements are proven only up to 14 points and for 24 (a proof for 15 is claimed in a 2026 preprint), so for the sizes of this family the best known packings come from computer search and a larger minimum angle is a new best packing.

papers.title: The densest packing of equal circles on a sphere
papers.task_relation: The task is the same packing problem for 58 circles, scored by the minimum angle. The paper's list goes to 90 circles (as Wang 2009 reports; this paper itself was not opened), the task family to 130, and the task's reference packing comes from Cohn's table of spherical codes.
papers.primary_goal: Compute the densest known packings of equal circles on a sphere for a range of numbers of circles.

papers.title: The closest packing of equal circles on a sphere
papers.task_relation: The task is the same packing problem for 58 circles; the paper's improved packings cover 20 to 40 circles, the task family 16 to 130.
papers.primary_goal: Find closest packings of circles on a sphere by minimising a repulsion energy and refining to exact solutions; it reports improved packings for 20 to 40 circles.
